title: Judges 14:10–20
context: At the wedding feast, Samson poses a riddle based on the lion and the honey, with a large wager. The Philistine companions threaten his wife, who presses Samson until he tells her the answer. Samson responds with a bitter insult and, empowered by the Spirit and burning with anger, kills thirty men in Ashkelon to pay the debt. His wife is then given to another man. Both traditions read the episode soberly, with moral clarity about Samson’s anger and violence and sympathy for his wife, while recognizing God’s purpose against the Philistines.

verses.text: His father went down to the woman; and Samson made a feast there, for the young men used to do so.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson’s father goes down to the woman, and Samson holds a feast, as young men customarily did. The Hebrew word for feast can suggest a drinking feast, though the text does not say Samson drank.

Arminian readers see Samson placing himself in settings that test his calling.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator notes the custom without comment. The feast sets the stage for the riddle.

Reformed readers likewise avoid assuming what the text does not say. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the setting, holding the details with caution.

verses.text: When they saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the Philistines see him, they bring thirty companions to be with him. The text does not explain why they were brought.

Arminian readers see the tension of a Danite at a Philistine wedding.
verses.reformedNotes:
The thirty companions surround Samson. Their motives are not stated.

Reformed readers see the setting of conflict taking shape around him. Both traditions read this plainly, noting that the companions become the audience and opponents for the riddle without speculating about their intentions beyond the text.

verses.text: Samson said to them, “Let me tell you a riddle now. If you can tell me the answer within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing;
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson poses a riddle: if they solve it within the seven days, he will give them thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing. The wager is large.

Arminian readers see Samson’s confidence and perhaps his pride.
verses.reformedNotes:
The riddle contest is a social game with real stakes. Samson sets the terms.

Reformed readers see an ordinary wedding custom turning into conflict. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the prize is significant enough to provoke serious pressure in the days ahead.

verses.text: but if you can’t tell me the answer, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing.” They said to him, “Tell us your riddle, that we may hear it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
If they cannot answer, they must give him the same. They accept and ask to hear the riddle.

Arminian readers see both sides freely entering the contest. The stakes are clear to everyone.
verses.reformedNotes:
The terms are reciprocal. The companions agree readily.

Reformed readers see the conflict escalating through human decisions. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, with the arrangement setting up the pressure placed on Samson’s wife and the violence that follows.

verses.text: He said to them, “Out of the eater came out food. Out of the strong came out sweetness.” They couldn’t in three days declare the riddle.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Out of the eater came out food. Out of the strong came out sweetness.” They cannot solve it in three days.

Arminian readers see the riddle drawn from Samson’s secret, which only he knows.
verses.reformedNotes:
The riddle depends on the lion and the honey, which no one else saw. It is nearly impossible to solve.

Reformed readers see Samson’s cleverness and his advantage. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note how the hidden act of verse 9 becomes the basis of a public contest.

verses.text: On the seventh day, they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband, that he may declare to us the riddle, lest we burn you and your father’s house with fire. Have you called us to impoverish us? Isn’t that so?”
verses.arminianNotes:
On the seventh day, the companions threaten Samson’s wife: entice him to reveal the riddle, or they will burn her and her father’s house. They accuse her of inviting them to be robbed.

Arminian readers see coercion and fear shaping her choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her situation is desperate; she is caught between her husband and her people. The threat is violent.

Reformed readers see sin spreading through intimidation. Both traditions read this with compassion for the woman and moral clarity about the companions’ threats.

verses.text: Samson’s wife wept before him, and said, “You just hate me, and don’t love me. You’ve told a riddle to the children of my people, and haven’t told it to me.” He said to her, “Behold, I haven’t told my father or my mother, so why should I tell you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson’s wife weeps, saying he hates her because he has not told her the riddle; he replies that he has not even told his parents. The relationship is strained.

Arminian readers see a marriage built on attraction rather than trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
She appeals to his love; he defends his secrecy. Neither fully trusts the other.

Reformed readers see the fragility of a marriage formed against wise counsel. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and with sympathy for the pressure the wife is under.

verses.text: She wept before him the seven days, while their feast lasted; and on the seventh day, he told her, because she pressed him severely; and she told the riddle to the children of her people.
verses.arminianNotes:
She weeps through the feast, and on the seventh day he tells her because she pressed him; she tells her people. Pressure wins.

Arminian readers see Samson yielding under persistent emotional pressure, a pattern that recurs with Delilah in chapter 16.
verses.reformedNotes:
Samson gives in, and she passes the answer on. The riddle’s secret is lost.

Reformed readers see a weakness that will prove costly again. Both traditions share this reading and note the wife’s own vulnerability under the threat of verse 15.

verses.text: The men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” He said to them, “If you hadn’t plowed with my heifer, you wouldn’t have found out my riddle.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men answer, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” Samson replies that they plowed with his heifer. His words are bitter and demeaning.

Arminian readers see anger and humiliation in his response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Samson knows how they learned the answer. His metaphor is crude and insulting toward his wife.

Reformed readers see sinful anger taking hold. Both traditions read this with moral clarity, neither excusing Samson’s words nor sensationalizing them, and note that his anger will soon turn violent.

verses.text: The LORD’s Spirit came mightily on him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck thirty men of them. He took their plunder, then gave the changes of clothing to those who declared the riddle. His anger burned, and he went up to his father’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Spirit comes mightily on him; he goes to Ashkelon, kills thirty men, takes their clothing, pays the debt, and returns home angry. Divine empowerment and human anger are both named.

Arminian readers see God using Samson against the Philistines while his anger remains his own.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator links the Spirit with the deed and anger with Samson. Interpreters differ on how to weigh these together.

Reformed readers see God accomplishing his purpose of 14:4 through a flawed deliverer. Both traditions read the violence soberly, without glorifying it.

verses.text: But Samson’s wife was given to his companion, who had been his friend.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson’s wife is given to his companion, who had been his friend. The marriage ends in betrayal and loss.

Arminian readers see the painful consequences of choices made without regard to wise counsel.
verses.reformedNotes:
The chapter ends with the wedding undone. The conflict will escalate in chapter 15.

Reformed readers see human failure and God’s larger purpose both moving the story forward. Both traditions read this as shared ground and with sympathy for the woman, who has little control over what happens to her.
